title: Path Portfolio Optimization: Defect, Lift, and the Price of Path Complexity

p.t: Classical portfolio theory takes a weight vector and a covariance matrix as primitives [35]. Everything path-dependent -momentum, drawdown control, trend, variance trading, lead-lag -arrives afterwards as a signal bolted onto a static optimizer. The alternative is to make the path the primitive: the signature is a universal coordinate system for continuous functionals of a path [3,33,29], and in those coordinates path-dependent and static allocation stop being different problems. The point of departure is Noguer i Alonso [39], which argues that geometricity is a first-order algebraic property whose obstructions are second order: a bracket when the lift is non-geometric, and a covariance when one averages over random paths. This paper asks what each obstruction does to a portfolio. Each turns out to be an object portfolio theory already prices under another name -and then, because being structurally elegant is not the same as being usable, it asks how much of the resulting advantage survives having to estimate anything. Spine. The covariance obstruction is risk; the bracket obstruction is execution; and the dimension of the strategy space is the price of admitting either. We call the resulting framework path portfolio optimization, by analogy with stochastic portfolio theory: where SPT takes the market weights as its primitive, path portfolio optimization takes the signature.

1. Excess growth is the geometricity defect (Corollary 13). The Marcus-forward lift gap at level two is one half the quadratic covariation; contracted with portfolio weights it is exactly Fernholz's γ * . Stochastic portfolio theory's central quantity is the bracket obstruction of Noguer i Alonso [39], and a portfolio theory written on a geometric lift has already spent it. 2. Direction is convention-free, risk and ruin are not (Corollaries 14,15). The antisymmetric level-two block is identical under both lifts pathwise, to machine precision, so no lead-lag estimate depends on the Itô/Marcus choice. The symmetric block does, and so does solvency: Marcus-lifted wealth cannot be extinguished by a jump, forward-lifted wealth can. Whether a model admits this representation of gap risk is determined by the chosen lift -that is, by the assumed execution convention -rather than by the dynamics alone. 3. The price of path complexity is dimensional, and it is paid in the symmetric block (Section 6). With E[S] known, level-two controls raise the certainty equivalent by 11.15× at d = 2 and 59.6× at d = 20; a word-class decomposition (Proposition 22) puts all of that gain in the symmetric words and exactly none of it in the antisymmetric ones. With E[S] estimated, the raw plug-in is negative below roughly six observations per parametermedian -306× the oracle at M/p = 1.19, with an interquartile range that does not come near zero -while ridge shrinkage that destroys half the value at d = 2 delivers 0.58× the oracle there. A model-consistent estimator that fits only the generator and rebuilds E[S] by exponential and shuffle recovers 0.95× at the same sample size (Proposition 23): the floor is a property of unstructured estimation of the risk form, not of path complexity.

The optimizer exists exactly when the class is coherently priced (Section 4). On the infinite-dimensional closure of the strategy space, the mean-variance value is finite if and only if µ ∈ Range(Γ 1/2 ) and attained if and only if µ ∈ Range(Γ); the maximal Sharpe ratio of the class is ∥Γ †/2 µ∥, and failure of the range condition is an asymptotic arbitrage inside the model. In log coordinates the leading obstruction to group-likeness of E[S] is exactly half the covariance of terminal increments (Proposition 9).

Self-exciting allocation closes, with a stated failure mode (Section 7). The Hawkes closure of Noguer i Alonso [39] makes myopic path-dependent allocation a linear solve in an augmented state. What fails near criticality is not the closure but the habit of substituting its stationary limit: at branching ratio 0.9 the stationary variance overstates the realized one by a factor of 4.9 on a twenty-unit horizon. 6. The cross-area is a signed, capped directional portfolio -but only against sign excitation (Section 8). It detects the sign of excitation asymmetry and is null under symmetric excitation; being reversal-odd, its edge is bounded by entropy production under the coarse-graining hypotheses of Proposition 31, which bind the one-step increments the cross-area accumulates rather than the path functional directly (Remark 32). The second negative result is that excitation which raises intensity without carrying direction moves the cross-area of the counting path (t = 15.99) and not that of the price path (t = 0.96). Reflexivity in activity and reflexivity in direction are different resources, and only the second is tradable. Related work. Signature-linear trading strategies with an exact shuffle-based mean-variance solution are due to Futter et al. [15], and linear path-functional portfolios in stochastic portfolio theory, with universality and convex tractability, to Cuchiero and Möller [7]; a kernel generalization is Futter et al. [16]. Relative to these, the present paper contributes no new optimizer. What it adds is a portfolio interpretation of the risk form through the geometricity defect and a connection between excess growth and the lift gap (Sections 3-5), the dimensional estimation study (Section 6), the corrected use of Hawkes closures (Section 7), and the activity-versusdirection decomposition of the cross-area trade (Section 8), whose statistic itself goes back to Gyurkó et al. [18]. The dimensional study stands in an explicit relation to the virtue-of-complexity result of Kelly et al. [25], spelled out in Remark 25.

What this paper is not. No market data is used anywhere. All parameters are invented and internally consistent. The estimation results are about sampling error only: transaction costs, non-stationarity and model misspecification would all make the picture worse, never better.

Let X : [0, T ] → R d be a log-price path of finite p-variation, possibly with jumps, S(X) 0,T its signature and S ≤m the truncation at level m. Words in {1, . . . , d} index coordinates, ⟨w, S⟩ is the coefficient of w, and ⊔ ⊔ is the shuffle product. The class is asymptotically unrestrictive: signature-linear functionals are dense in continuous functionals on compacta of unparameterized paths, the standard universality argument behind signature methods in finance [29,23,32,8]. Level one reproduces buy-and-hold. Level two reproduces T 0 X i dX j -momentum when i = j, lead-lag when i ̸ = j. Everything a practitioner calls "a signal times a position" lives at level two or above. Throughout, p = d + d 2 denotes the number of level-≤ 2 words, the parameter count of the problem.

Definition 2 (Defect form). Proposition 3 (Defect form is covariance; Proved, known). For a geometric lift with E∥S ≤2m ∥ < ∞ and words u, v of length at most m, D(u, v) = Cov(⟨u, S⟩, ⟨v, S⟩); hence Proof. The shuffle identity ⟨u, S⟩⟨v, S⟩ = ⟨u⊔ ⊔v, S⟩ holds pathwise; take expectations and subtract the product of means. Words in u ⊔ ⊔ v have length at most 2m.

The coordinate statement has a coordinate-free form. In the shuffle Hopf algebra the shuffle product is adjoint to the deconcatenation coproduct ∆ [40], so with S = E[S(X)] the whole defect form is the single tensor Group-likeness is the equation ∆g = g ⊗ g, so D = 0 iff S is group-like -the degeneracy half of Corollary 6 becomes definitional. And since a geometric signature is group-like pathwise, ∆S = S ⊗ S, while ∆ commutes with expectation, the covariance tensor of the signature: Proposition 3 in two lines, with no words. The coordinate proof is retained above because it shows where the truncation level 2m enters.

). This is not new, and two lines of work make it precise. Futter et al. [15] represent a trading strategy as a linear functional of the signature and solve the resulting mean-variance problem in closed form, with the variance computed exactly by shuffling against an expected signature; Equation (1) below is the static special case of their Theorem 3.1. Cuchiero and Möller [7] introduce linear path-functional portfolios in stochastic portfolio theory, prove their universality, and observe that mean-variance and log-wealth optimization over the class reduce to convex quadratic programs. Shuffle-based moment computations against expected signatures are likewise standard in signature pricing and execution [23,32,8], and the grouplikeness characterization in Corollary 6 is the expected-signature theory of Lyons and Ni [31] and Chevyrev and Lyons [4]. The proposition is stated here as shared infrastructure, not a contribution. What this paper adds downstream of it is the reading of D as the geometricity defect of Noguer i Alonso [39] -so that risk is literally the failure of the mean path to be a path -and the estimation study of Section 6, which neither of the works above carries out.

D is symmetric positive semidefinite, and D ≡ 0 if and only if E[S(X)] is group-like, which holds if and only if the reduced path is deterministic. So an expected signature is a legitimate path exactly when there is no risk to price. Take d = 2, T = 1, X t = bt + σW t with b = (0.06, 0.02) ⊤ and Σ = ( 0.040 0.012 0.012 0.090 ), so that E[S T ] = exp(T (b + 1 2 Σ)) in closed form. Against 200,000 simulated paths the closed-form coordinates E[S 1 ] = 0.060000, E[S 12 ] = 0.006600, E[S 1122 ] = 0.000480 return 0.060126, 0.006738, 0.000475. The defect form computed from E[S] alone reproduces the sample covariance of the six level-≤ 2 payoffs to a maximum relative deviation of 0.0036; its eigenvalues are all strictly positive with condition number 134.3; on a deterministic path it returns 2.78 × 10 -17 , confirming Corollary 6. The pathwise shuffle identity holds to 2.0 × 10 -15 and Chen concatenation to 6.7 × 10 -16 . At γ = 3 the optimizer (1) gives ℓ * = (0.0448, 0.0007, 7.9375, -1.1689, -1.1689, 3.8578) on the basis ((1), (2), (11), ( 12), ( 21), ( 22)), with predicted mean and variance 0.334685 and 0.111562 against realized 0.333902 and 0.111666. The weights on (12) and (21) are numerically identical, so the antisymmetric -Lévy area -component of the optimal control is exactly zero: under a driver whose area has zero mean the optimizer declines to trade direction and holds only the symmetric, variance-like combination. Section 8 is that observation with the mean put back in. The largest weight sits on (11). Under a geometric lift the shuffle relation makes that word exactly 1 2 (X 1 T -X 1 0 ) 2 , the squared terminal log return, whose mean is dominated by the variance: the gain comes from convexity, not forecasting. It is not the variance swap [X 1 , X 1 ] T , which by Proposition 33 enters the investable universe only under the forward lift -a distinction Section 6 shows to be the whole content of the level-two premium.

p.s: The Hilbert geometry of the strategy space
p.t: The finite truncation of Section 3 sits inside an infinite-dimensional problem, and making that explicit settles a question the finite statement quietly assumes: when does the optimizer (1) exist at all? Fix summable weights ω w > 0 and let H ω be the Hilbert space of coefficient sequences ℓ = (ℓ w ) w with ∥ℓ∥ 2 = w ℓ 2 w ω w < ∞, so that Φ(X) = (⟨w, S(X)⟩) w is the signature feature map and G ℓ = ⟨ℓ, Φ(X)⟩ Hω . Under moment bounds on E∥S∥ 2 the covariance operator Γ = E[(Φ -EΦ) ⊗ (Φ -EΦ)] is trace-class, self-adjoint and positive; the defect form is its coordinate expression, and the mean signature µ = EΦ is the mean embedding of the path law in the sense of kernel mean embeddings [38], with the signature kernel [26,41] as the reproducing kernel. Theorem 7 (Existence and value; Proved). Let Γ be a positive self-adjoint trace-class operator on a separable Hilbert space and γ > 0. Then and when the supremum is finite it is attained if and only if µ ∈ Range(Γ), with maximizer ℓ * = γ -1 Γ † µ. Proof. If µ has a component µ 0 ̸ = 0 in ker Γ, then ℓ = tµ 0 makes the objective t∥µ 0 ∥ 2 , unbounded. Otherwise diagonalize Γ = k λ k e k ⊗ e k with λ k > 0 on (ker Γ) ⊥ ; the objective separates across coordinates, each one-dimensional supremum is µ 2 k /(2γλ k ), and the total is finite exactly when k µ 2 k /λ k < ∞, i.e. µ ∈ Range(Γ 1/2 ). The coordinatewise maximizer is ℓ k = µ k /(γλ k ), which lies in H ω exactly when k µ 2 k /λ 2 k < ∞, i.e. µ ∈ Range(Γ).

p.s: The Hilbert geometry of the strategy space
p.t: In the diagonalization of the proof, the condition µ ∈ Range(Γ 1/2 ) reads k ⟨µ, e k ⟩ 2 /λ k < ∞: it is the Picard condition of linear inverse problems [11], with the frontier slope of Corollary 8 as the regularized solution norm. Portfolio choice on path space is, in this exact sense, an inverse problem: the market supplies the operator, the mean embedding supplies the data, and asymptotic arbitrage is what ill-posedness looks like in finance. The gap between the two range conditions is not a technicality. If µ ∈ Range(Γ 1/2 )\Range(Γ), the value is finite but approached only along a sequence of ever-larger controls: the strategy class contains approximate optimizers and no optimizer. And if µ / ∈ Range(Γ 1/2 ), the class contains payoff directions whose Sharpe ratio is unbounded -an asymptotic arbitrage inside the model. The condition µ ∈ Range(Γ 1/2 ) is therefore the path-space statement that the market prices the strategy class coherently. Corollary 8 (Signature efficient frontier; Proved). For c > 0, max{⟨ℓ, µ⟩ : ⟨ℓ, Γℓ⟩ ≤ c} = √ c ∥Γ †/2 µ∥ whenever the right side is finite. The efficient frontier in (risk, mean) coordinates is the ray of slope ∥Γ †/2 µ∥: the maximal Sharpe ratio of the class is the norm whose finiteness Theorem 7 characterizes.

The slogan behind Corollary 6 -risk is the failure of the mean path to be a path -admits an exact leading-order form. Group-like elements are exponentials of Lie elements, and at level two the Lie part is antisymmetric; so the symmetric level-two component of log E[S] is precisely the lowest-order obstruction to group-likeness.

For any geometric lift with square-integrable leveltwo signature, the symmetric part of the level-two component of log E[S(X)] equals 1 2 Cov(X T -X 0 ), which is one half the level-one block of the defect form D. Proof. Pathwise, the shuffle identity at level two gives So in log coordinates the leading non-Lie component of the expected signature is the covariance of terminal increments, halved: risk is literally the first thing one meets on the way from E[S] back to the group. The identity is distribution-free, and holds numerically on a two-point-mixture driver to 1.1 × 10 -7 on objects of size 4.5 × 10 -2 .

p.s: Corollary 10 (Distance to geometricity in the log chart; Proved).
p.t: At truncation level two, the Lie algebra g 2 = {(a, A) : a ∈ R d , A antisymmetric} is a linear subspace of log coordinates, and the Euclidean distance from log E[S] to g 2 is exactly 1 2 ∥ Cov(X T -X 0 )∥ F . The distance from the expected signature to the group-like variety, measured in the log chart, is half the Frobenius norm of the covariance of terminal increments. Proof. Orthogonal projection onto g 2 removes exactly the symmetric level-two block of the log; Proposition 9 identifies that block as 1 2 Cov(X T -X 0 ). Group-like elements form a variety, not a subspace, so "distance to geometricity" needs a chart to be well defined; the log chart is the natural one because it linearizes the variety, and in it the distance is not merely bounded by the covariance -it is the covariance, halved. The projection onto g 2 used in the proof is, at level two, the first Eulerian idempotent of the tensor algebra [40], so the corollary sits inside the canonical Lie-theoretic decomposition rather than being an ad hoc matrix split; at higher truncation levels the same idempotent defines the projection, and the resulting distance formula is open.

p.s: Log utility and the Kelly ray
p.t: Proposition 11 (Second-order Kelly control; Proved). Let terminal wealth be 1 + G ℓ . Then and the second-order log-optimal control is The Kelly control lies on the same ray as every mean-variance optimizer -the efficient-frontier ray of Corollary 8 -shrunk by one plus the squared maximal Sharpe ratio of the class. ) and E[G 2 ℓ ] = ⟨ℓ, Γℓ⟩ + ⟨ℓ, µ⟩ 2 ; the second display is Sherman-Morrison. Dropping the ⟨ℓ, µ⟩ 2 term would return the γ = 1 mean-variance control exactly; the correct expansion keeps the direction and shrinks the scale. The expansion is formal in ∥ℓ∥: by Corollary 15 the argument 1 + G ℓ need not be positive for every control under the forward lift, so the statement is to be read on a neighbourhood of ℓ = 0, or under a geometric lift where wealth is an exponential and the logarithm is never evaluated off its domain. So the Kelly criterion, Markowitz, and signature optimization coincide in direction on path space and differ only in how far along the frontier ray they sit; the universal-portfolio reading of the same ray is Cover [5], and exact (rather than second-order) log-optimal signature portfolios are the object approximated in Cuchiero and Möller [7].

p.s: The lift is the execution convention
p.t: Theorem 12 (Lift gap at level two; Proved). With S M the Marcus (geometric) and S F the forward iterated-sums level-two signature of the same stream, S M,ij -S F,ij = 1 2 [X i , X j ] T : the lifts differ only in their symmetric block, by one half the quadratic covariation. For continuous semimartingales this is the Itô-Stratonovich correction; on pure-jump streams it is Hoffman's exponential [22,34], the algebraic content of the Hopf square of Noguer i Alonso [39]. Simulation confirms both: with 20,000 paths of 1000 steps the mean level-two difference is ( 0.020011 0.006002 0.006002 0.044993 ) against 1 2 ΣT = ( 0.020 0.006 0.006 0.045 ), maximum error 10 -5 ; on a pure-jump stream S M -S F = 1 2 ∆X ∆X ⊤ holds to 1.7 × 10 -15 .

p.s: Corollary 13 (Excess growth is the geometricity defect; Proved).
p.t: For weights π held fixed across a log-price move u, whose leading term is -γ * π for the rank-one covariance uu ⊤ . In the continuous limit log V T - ); the bracket is 2γ * π for vv ⊤ . For the continuous statement, let S i = e X i with X a continuous semimartingale, and let V be the self-financing wealth of the constant-weight portfolio, The first term integrates to π ⊤ (X T -X 0 ), the level-one signature coordinate, which is identical under both lifts. The second term is exactly the contraction of the level-two lift gap of Theorem 12 with the tensor diag(π) -ππ ⊤ : So the entire difference between logarithmic wealth and the level-one signature flow is the lift gap read through one fixed portfolio tensor; the map π → diag(π) -ππ ⊤ is how the bracket obstruction enters the one-dimensional wealth process. Both displays put γ * on the same side. The one-period portfolio return exceeds the level-one coordinate by γ * , and continuously rebalanced wealth exceeds π ⊤ d log X by γ * dt: what carries no rebalancing premium is the level-one signature flow itself, not either wealth process. The elementary check is π = ( 1 2 , 1 2 ) and u = (a, -a), where the level-one coordinate is zero and the executed return is log cosh a ≈ a 2 /2 = γ * .

p.s: Corollary 13 (Excess growth is the geometricity defect; Proved).
p.t: The continuous identity is classical [13,14]; the placement is the point. Excess growth is not a rebalancing artifact that stochastic portfolio theory happens to isolate -it is the geometricity defect of the portfolio map, the same bracket obstruction as in Theorem 12. Signatures have been brought into stochastic portfolio theory before, as a universal parameterization of path-dependent portfolio weights [7]; the identification made here runs in the other direction, reading SPT's central scalar as a statement about the lift of the signature itself, and to our knowledge it has not been stated.

The antisymmetric part of the level-two signature is identical under both lifts, pathwise; measured discrepancy 6.5 × 10 -16 . Arguments about Itô versus Stratonovich versus Marcus can change the sign and size of a variance-trading or rebalancing P&L. They cannot touch a lead-lag estimate. Corollary 15 (Ruin is a convention; Proved). Marcus-lifted wealth exp(π ⊤ u) is strictly positive for every bounded control and finite move; forward-lifted wealth 1 + π ⊤ (e u -1) is non-positive whenever π ⊤ (e u -1) ≤ -1, attainable at one jump for levered π. A levered portfolio rebalanced continuously through a crash cannot go bankrupt at a jump, because it is always selling into the fall; executed at the jump it can. Any risk system built on a geometric lift has silently assumed away the event it most needs to measure.

Everything so far assumes E[S] is known. It is not. Because Proposition 3 makes D a covariance of p = d + d 2 payoffs, the plug-in policy l = (γ D) -1 μ inherits the pathology that Michaud [37] and DeMiguel et al. [10] document for mean-variance in the static case -with the difference that p now grows quadratically in d. The experiments below estimate μ and D from M independent paths, form l, and evaluate its true certainty equivalent CE( l) = µ ⊤ lγ 2 l⊤ D l against the exact (µ, D). Calibrations. Both drivers are X t = bt + σW t on [0, 1] under a geometric lift at γ = 3, so E[S] = exp(T (b + 1 2 Σ)) is exact and D is assembled from it by shuffling. At d = 2, the calibration of Section 3.1: p = 6, cond D = 134.3. At d = 20, volatilities equally spaced on [0.22, 0.35], equicorrelation 0.40, drifts equally spaced on [0.04, 0.10]: p = 420, cond D = 1906 with 81.0% of the eigenvalues above 10 -3 λ max . The population problem is well posed at both sizes, so everything below is a sample-size statement and not a conditioning statement. Four policies. Raw is the unregularized plug-in. Ridge replaces D by D + δ λI with λ = tr D/p, at two intensities: the fixed δ = 0.25 of identity-target shrinkage [27], and δ = p/M , the ambiguity radius that Proposition 24 and the Marchenko-Pastur discussion below both prescribe. Model is a model-consistent plug-in: it estimates only the generator ( b, Σ) from the level-one increments and rebuilds μ and D from it by tensor exponential and shuffle. The level-one plug-in is carried throughout as a benchmark. Cells report medians over independent replications, with interquartile ranges and Pr[CE < 0], because in the regime that matters the loss is heavy-tailed and its mean is not a stable summary.

Before the tables, one identity organizes everything in them. Proposition 16 (Exact loss decomposition; Proved). For any ℓ, for any estimator l: the expected plug-in loss is the D-weighted mean squared error of the weights, with no higher-order terms. Proof. CE is a concave quadratic with maximizer ℓ * ; expand around it. The identity is why the tables behave as they do. The plug-in error l -ℓ * contains D-1 , so its D-weighted second moment inherits the spectrum of the inverse sample covariance. Two facts locate the barrier without any distributional assumption. First, rank( D) ≤ M -1 exactly, so M ≥ p + 1 is necessary for the raw plug-in to be defined at all -linear algebra, not asymptotics. Second, for pure noise with finite fourth moments the sample spectrum concentrates on the Marchenko-Pastur bulk [(1 -p/M ) 2 , (1 + p/M ) 2 ] [36], so the smallest eigenvalue collapses as M ↓ p and ∥ D-1 ∥ diverges together with the loss of Proposition 16; the measured edge tracks the bound across M/p from 1.3 to 200. Signature coordinates are neither independent nor identically distributed across levels, so Marchenko-Pastur is a located analogy, not a theorem about D; the rank statement needs no such caveat. The random-matrix toolkit for cleaning sample covariance matrices in finance is surveyed by Bun et al. [2]; what is specific here is that the payoffs whose covariance is being cleaned are generated algebraically, by words, rather than observed, so their number is chosen by the truncation level and not by the data.

The exact finite-sample theory of Kan and Zhou [24] is the natural thing to reach for here, and it is worth being precise about how far it reaches. It is exact for the level-one sub-problem, where the payoffs are Gaussian and D is Wishart, and there it predicts the divergence of the expected plug-in loss as M ↓ p. It does not transfer to level two: those payoffs are quadratic in Gaussians, D is not Wishart, and we have no closed form for the negative entries of Table 2. Those entries are measured, not derived, which is why they are reported with dispersion. The rate itself can be stated as a theorem, with hypotheses the signature setting makes natural -and with the dimension entering through the trace and the conditioning of D rather than through the word count. The word count p appears nowhere in the display. Bounding tr D ≤ B 2 p recovers the familiar p/M rate, but Remark 18 shows that bound to be wasteful exactly in the signature setting; the operative ratio is tr(D)/(λ 0 M ). Proof. By Proposition 16 it suffices to bound ∥D 1/2 ( l -ℓ * )∥. With D centred at the population mean the identity l -ℓ * = γ -1 D-1 (μ -µ) -γ( D -D)ℓ * is exact; sample centring perturbs D by (μ -µ)(μ -µ) ⊤ , of operator norm O P (1/M ), which contributes below the stated order. The intrinsic-dimension form of matrix Bernstein [42,43] gives ∥ D -D∥ op ≤ λ 0 /2 with probability 1 -δ/2 once M ≥ C 0 log(intdim(V )/δ), and on that event ∥ D-1 ∥ ≤ 2/λ 0 . Vector Bernstein gives ∥μ -µ∥ 2 ≲ (tr D + B 2 log(1/δ))/M , and matrix Bernstein gives ∥( D -D)ℓ * ∥ 2 ≲ B 4 ∥ℓ * ∥ 2 (1 + log(1/δ))/M , which is dimension-free. Combining terms gives the display; the μ term carries the trace.

The theorem is an upper bound under hypothesis (ii), which is a statement about D. What fails in the tables is λ min ( D), not λ min (D): the good event of the proof is exactly what a sample of size M ≈ p does not deliver. So the theorem and the tables are not two readings of one quantity -the first bounds the loss once the sample resolves the spectrum, the second measures what happens before it does. Remark 18 (Effective dimension, and where the difficulty actually lives). On paths of 1-variation at most R the factorial decay |⟨w, S⟩| ≤ R |w| /|w|! gives tr(D) ≤ k≤m d k R 2k /(k!) 2 , a series that converges even as m → ∞: the trace side of the sample-size floor does not grow with the truncation level at all, and neither does the intrinsic dimension, which is 1.49 at d = 2 and 3.84 at d = 20 here against word counts of 6 and 420. The difficulty migrates into the conditioningλ min (D) decays factorially across levels and the constants carry λ -2 0 -so what the trace saves, the spectrum spends. The operative quantity is the effective dimension d eff = tr(D)/λ min (D), equal to 200 at d = 2 and 7325 at d = 20. It summarizes the tables better than p does: the raw plug-in reaches 85% of its oracle value at M = 0.62 d eff in the pair and M = 0.68 d eff in the cross section, whereas the corresponding values of M/p, namely 20.8 and 11.9, differ by a factor of 1.8. This is a measured statement about two calibrations, not a theorem.

The fixed intensity δ = 0.25 destroys half the attainable value at p = 6 (0.49-0.50 of oracle at every sample size, against 0.998 for the raw plug-in at M = 8000) and is the difference between -306× and +0.58× the oracle at p = 420, M = 500. p.s: Remark 19 (Bias-variance across truncation levels). The oracle value CE *
p.t: Proposition 22 (Where the level-two premium lives; Conditional, measured). On both calibrations the entire level-≤ 2 oracle gain sits in the symmetric block. The antisymmetric block adds exactly nothing: under these drivers its mean vanishes and it is uncorrelated with every This changes what the dimensional trade-off is a statement about. Under a geometric lift the shuffle relation makes the symmetric level-two block exactly 1 2 ∆X ⊗ ∆X, a quadratic function of the terminal increment; only the antisymmetric block -the Lévy area -is genuinely path-dependent. So what level two buys on these drivers is convexity in the terminal return, and the path-dependent half of the level earns nothing here, by construction: the driver has no expected area. Section 8 is where the antisymmetric words are put in front of a driver that pays them. That the antisymmetric block earns exactly zero here is a statement about the driverwhich is time-reversible and has no expected area -and not a statement about markets. And by Proposition 33 the genuine variance swap [X, X] T is not in this universe at all -it enters only under the forward lift. The honest name for the 59.64× is therefore the price of admitting quadratic payoffs in the terminal increment. The cross section beats the pair because it has d(d + 1)/2 of them rather than three -though only just: the count rises from three to two hundred and ten while the value rises tenfold, so on equicorrelated assets the marginal quadratic direction is worth very little, and it is the estimation cost that scales with the count.

p.s: Remark 19 (Bias-variance across truncation levels). The oracle value CE *
p.t: Second, the estimation problem gets worse faster. The oracle advantage grows roughly linearly in d here while p grows quadratically, so the sample size required to realize the advantage outruns the advantage itself. This is a tradability statement: path complexity survives only where the sample does. Third -and this is the practical inversion -how much to regularize is not a matter of taste. At d = 2 a practitioner who shrinks at fixed intensity is throwing away half the value. At d = 20 the same practitioner is the only one still solvent. Conditioning is not the culprit: the population problem is well posed at both sizes, as the calibration paragraph records. The failure is a sample-size failure, which is why shrinkage -and not a better inversion -is what repairs it.

p.s: The floor is a property of the estimator
p.t: It is tempting to look for the repair in the algebra rather than in shrinkage, since the shuffle relations are exact constraints linking the coordinates of E[S]. They give nothing here, and the reason is worth stating: those relations hold pathwise, so any sample-based D satisfies every one of them identically. There is no violated constraint to project onto. What the algebra does supply is an assembly map -from a generator to E[S] by tensor exponential, and from E[S] to D by shuffling -and that map becomes an estimator as soon as one is willing to name a driver class. Proposition 23 (Model-consistent estimation removes the floor; Conditional, measured). Estimating only ( b, Σ) from the level-one increments -d + d(d + 1)/2 numbers, 230 at d = 20 against 420 free means and 88,410 free covariance entries -and rebuilding μ = exp(T ( b + 1 2 Σ)) and D from it by shuffling recovers 0.950 of the oracle at M/p = 1.19 and 0.999 at M/p = 47.6, where the raw plug-in reads -306× and 0.973. At d = 2 it recovers 0.957 at M = 60. The sample-size floor of Proposition 20 is therefore a property of unstructured estimation of the risk form, not of path complexity. The caveat is exactly as large as the claim. The model-consistent estimator is evaluated under a correctly specified driver, so what it measures is the cost of not using a model, not the cost of using the wrong one; under misspecification its bias does not vanish with M and the comparison would invert at some sample size we do not identify. What survives the caveat is the decomposition: the -306× of Table 2 is the price of estimating 420 × 421/2 second moments freely, and it is not a statement about level-two words as such.

p.s: The floor is a property of the estimator
p.t: The ridge itself deserves a better pedigree than "the fix that works". Proposition 24 (Shrinkage is priced ambiguity; Proved). Consider the robust problem In particular, with r µ = 0 the robust optimizer is exactly the ridge policy ℓ R = γ( D + r D I) -1 μ, and a mean radius r µ > 0 adds a norm penalty on top. Proof. This closes the loop with the tables, and the two ridge columns are the two sides of it. The intensity δ = p/M is the covariance-ambiguity radius that the Marchenko-Pastur discussion prescribes for sampling noise, and it behaves as a priced ambiguity should: it shrinks away as the sample grows, so the policy converges. The fixed δ = 0.25 is not a radius at all -it prices an ambiguity that does not shrink, which is why it is flat in every row of both tables, better than the radius when the sample is smallest and worse than it forever after. In the robust reading [17], Proposition 21's sign flip says the fair ambiguity premium is negligible at p = 6 and is the entire game at p = 420. Shrinkage is not a numerical hack; it is the price of not knowing D, and on these calibrations the price scales with p/M . Remark 25 (Relation to the virtue of complexity). Read on its own, this section looks like the reverse of Kelly et al. [25], who prove in a high-dimensional ridge-regularized return-prediction model that expected out-of-sample performance can keep improving as the parameter count passes the number of observations, and that with sufficient shrinkage the non-monotonicity at the interpolation point disappears entirely. The two pictures are the same picture. The catastrophic column of Table 2 is the unregularized policy evaluated in the neighbourhood of the interpolation point, which is exactly where the ridgeless limit of a high-dimensional linear problem degenerates [20]; and their virtue statement is conditional on shrinkage, as is ours -the p/M -ridged level-≤ 2 policy never loses to the static one at any sample size tested. Two differences are worth keeping. Their complexity is a free parameter, dialled by adding random features to a fixed information set, whereas p m (d) here is fixed by the truncation level and the cross-sectional width, so complexity is inherited rather than chosen. And their asymptotics hold the complexity ratio fixed, while Proposition 23 says that in this setting the ratio can be sidestepped: naming the driver class buys at M/p = 1.19 what shrinkage alone does not buy until far later. Where complexity is a virtue it is a virtue bought with regularization -statistical in their setting, algebraic in ours.

For exponential Hawkes drivers [21,1] the truncated expected signature admits a finite-dimensional linear closure after state-weight augmentation [39]. Writing Z t for the augmented state, the conditional objects µ t = µ(Z t ) and D t = D(Z t ) are available in closed form, so: Proposition 26 (Myopic feedback policy; Proved). Under the closure, the mean-varianceoptimal signature-linear control re-solved at each t is ℓ * t = (γD t ) -1 µ t , a deterministic function of the augmented state. Path-dependent allocation under self-excitation is a linear solve in Z t , not a stochastic control problem. Remark 27 (Beyond myopia; Conjectural). For a general utility the candidate optimal control has the Merton form ℓ t = -Vw Vww D(Z t ) -1 µ(Z t ), with Proposition 26 the constant-relative-tolerance special case in which the hedging demand vanishes. We do not assert this: the augmented state jumps, so the value function solves a partial integro-differential equation rather than a diffusion HJB, and a verification theorem on the state space of the closure is open. The myopic statement is what is proved; the Merton form is what a companion paper should prove. This is a myopic feedback rule -optimal one period at a time, with no hedging demand for future variation in Z. We do not solve the intertemporal problem, and Section 3.1 and Section 6 are both static optimizations over a path-dependent payoff basis. Saying otherwise would overstate what is here.

A separate warning concerns how the closure is used in practice. For a scalar clock with baseline µ, decay β and branching ratio n the stationary limits are E[N T ] → µT /(1 -n) and Var(N T ) → µT /(1 -n) 3 , and it is tempting to substitute them. Proposition 28 (Stationary substitution error; Proved for the first moment, measured for the second). Integrating the closure forward from λ 0 = µ gives the exact finite-horizon first moment whose relaxation time is τ = (β(1 -n)) -1 . The stationary limit is the T /τ → ∞ truncation of (2); all of the error in Table 4 is the truncation, not the closure. Formula (2) and its second-moment companion are classical: (N t , λ t ) is an affine point process whose moments solve linear ODEs [12,9], and the closure of Noguer i Alonso [39] recovers exactly this system as the level-one block of the state-weight-augmented expected signature. Table 4 separates the two failure modes. Formula (2) reproduces the simulated mean to within 1.3% across the whole range of branching ratios, and integrating the second-moment system likewise reproduces the simulated variance to within 2.5%; the stationary substitution is wrong by 65.8% in the mean and 388.2% in the variance at n = 0.9. The closure of Noguer i Alonso [39] is therefore not the source of the problem, and the apparent near-critical breakdown of expected-signature methods is an artifact of how they are usually applied. The correct instruction is not to distrust the closure but to integrate it.

p.t: , each summand is one-step measurable for the chain that carries the current levels alongside the internal state, and that chain is stationary only under a further assumption on the levels. So the ceiling binds the sign channel of the increments the cross-area accumulates; it is not a bound on E[A ij ] itself, and we do not claim one. The Markov premise is an assumption about the coarse-graining, not a measured fact, and Pinsker is loose. The structural claim survives the constant: excitation asymmetry is simultaneously the source of the edge and the entropy production that caps it, and there is no configuration in which one is large and the other small.

p.s: Dimension and what the lift buys
p.t: A control of order m has N m = k≤m d k coordinates; under a geometric lift the shuffle relations cut the free directions to the free nilpotent dimension L m = k≤m 1 k e|k µ(e)d k/e [40], with L m /N m equal to 0.500, 0.355, 0.263 at m = 2, 3, 4 for d = 5 and 0.500, 0.347, 0.257 for d = 10. Proposition 33 (Level-two complement; Proved). At m = 2 the forward lift breaks the shuffle relation S ij + S ji = S i S j by exactly -[X i , X j ] T , so the N 2 -L 2 = d(d + 1)/2 additional directions available under the forward lift are spanned by the quadratic-covariation payoffs -the variance and covariance swaps. Both identities verified to 2.2 × 10 -15 at d = 4, where N 2 = 20, L 2 = 10. Remark 34 (Conjectural). That the analogous statement holds at every m -the full N m -L m complement being spanned by iterated-bracket functionals of the quadratic covariation -is plausible from the Hopf square of Noguer i Alonso [39] but is not proved here, and nothing in this paper depends on it. The practical content is that choosing a lift is choosing whether the volatility surface is in the investable universe. A geometric-lift theory is more parsimonious and cannot express variance trading; a forward-lift theory is larger and can, at the cost of d(d + 1)/2 more parameterswhich, by Section 6, is not a cost to be waved through.

The three difficulties of the title enter through three identities that do not interact at the orders computed: geometry through D = Cov and its Hilbert closure (Proposition 3, Theorem 7); execution through 1 2 [X, X] T contracted with diag(π)ππ ⊤ (Theorem 12, Corollary 13); estimation through the exact loss γ 2 ∥D 1/2 ( l -ℓ * )∥ 2 at rate tr(D)/(λ 0 M ) (Proposition 16, Theorem 17). We state this as a synthesis rather than a theorem: each identity is exact on its own, and their joint content is that each obstruction has its own currency -a tensor block, a portfolio tensor, a sample ratio -and none can be paid in another's.

Proved. Proposition 3 (known) and Corollary 6; Theorem 7, Corollary 8, Propositions 9 and 16; Corollary 10, Proposition 11 to second order, Proposition 24, and Theorem 17 under its hypotheses (i)-(ii); Theorem 12 and Corollaries 13-15; Proposition 26 as a myopic statement; Proposition 33 at m = 2; Proposition 28 for the first moment, with its second-moment analogue integrated numerically rather than in closed form; the dimension counts. Conditional. Propositions 20, 21, 22 and 23 are measured on two calibrations at one risk aversion; the thresholds are indicative, not universal. Proposition 31 rests on the Markov and one-step-measurability premises stated with it, is false without them, and by Remark 32 applies to the increments of the cross-area rather than to the cross-area itself. Propositions 29 and 30 are proved for the simulated families only. Both the Marchenko-Pastur localization of the estimation barrier and the appeal to Kan and Zhou [24] are analogies: the first has an exact rank statement attached, the second is exact only for the level-one sub-problem, since level-two payoffs are quadratic in Gaussians and D is not Wishart. The effective-dimension reading of Remark 18 is a measured regularity across two calibrations, not a theorem. The Merton form of the remark in Section 7 is conjectural. Conjectural. The general-m complement (Remark after Proposition 33); and that the M/p threshold is stable across drift and covariance structures other than the two used here.

No market data anywhere; all parameters invented. The Gaussian driver in Sections 3.1 and 6 is i.i.d. across replications, so the estimation results measure sampling error only and understate the difficulty under non-stationarity. Transaction costs appear nowhere; the level-two words are exactly the high-turnover ones, so Section 6 is an upper bound on realizable value. Neither ridge intensity was tuned; a tuned or nonlinear shrinkage [28] would dominate both. The model-consistent policy of Proposition 23 is evaluated under a correctly specified driver and therefore measures the cost of not using a model, never the cost of using a wrong one; nothing here bounds its bias under misspecification. The word-class attribution of Proposition 22 is for drivers with zero expected area, which is why the antisymmetric block earns nothing in it; a driver with excitation asymmetry moves value into that block, and Section 8 measures that separately rather than jointly. The cross-area magnitudes of Proposition 29 are activity, not P&L; Section 8.1 gives the traded version, where the tick size is fixed and the sign-copying probability q is imposed rather than estimated from any market. Nothing shows any strategy attains the entropy bound. Scope. The theoretical conclusions should be interpreted as a framework for organizing pathdependent portfolio construction rather than as a claim of immediate economic profitability. The simulations isolate estimation error and structural effects in controlled environments. A market implementation would additionally require transaction-cost modeling, turnover constraints, robust estimation, out-of-sample validation, and comparison against simpler benchmark strategies.
